notice: Independently authored practice questions. Not official Anthropic exam content and not drawn from any exam.

questions.scenario: Harbourline Credit Union's operations director asks for 'an AI agent that handles member disputes end to end'. Discovery shows that 70% of disputes fall into five card-chargeback reason codes with fixed evidence checklists, while the remainder need judgement across several back-office systems.
questions.question: Which initial solution framing best translates this business problem into a Claude-based design?

options.A: A workflow that classifies each dispute by reason code, has Claude assemble the evidence checklist and draft the case summary, and routes the non-standard remainder to analysts
options.B: A single autonomous agent with access to every back-office system so it can handle all disputes uniformly
options.C: A fine-tuned classifier only, because chargebacks are a classification problem and generation adds no value
options.D: A chat assistant for members to self-serve dispute status, deferring internal process changes

questions.explanation: Translating a business request starts from the shape of the work, not from the label the sponsor used. When most volume follows known, enumerable steps, a code-orchestrated workflow with Claude doing classification and evidence summarisation delivers value quickly, is testable and keeps cost predictable. The judgement-heavy remainder can be routed to people (or a later, narrower agent) once the workflow has produced data about those cases. Starting with a fully autonomous agent for everything maximises risk and cost for the part of the problem that does not need autonomy.

why_incorrect.B: Uniform autonomy over every system adds cost, latency and excessive agency for the 70% of cases that follow fixed steps; it also makes failures harder to test and audit.
why_incorrect.C: Classification is one step, but the business value comes from evidence assembly and summarisation, which a classifier alone does not provide.
why_incorrect.D: This addresses a different problem (member status queries) and leaves the analyst workload the sponsor described untouched.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health wants to reduce the time nurses spend writing discharge summaries. The draft must reflect the structured EHR record, never invent medications, and be signed by a clinician. Leadership asks you to identify which requirements should drive the architecture.
questions.question: Which TWO requirements most directly shape the Claude solution architecture? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Medications in the summary must come only from the structured EHR record, which implies grounding the prompt in that data and validating the output against it
options.B: Summaries should use a warm, plain-language tone for patients
options.C: A clinician must review and sign each summary, which implies a human approval step and an audit trail before filing
options.D: The team prefers the most capable model available so quality is never in question
options.E: The nurse UI should match the existing EHR colour scheme

questions.explanation: Architecturally significant requirements are the ones that constrain structure. 'Never invent medications' forces grounding: the medication list should be passed from the structured record (and ideally validated against it after generation) rather than left to free generation. 'Signed by a clinician' forces a human approval step and an audit trail before anything is filed. Preferences about tone or UI colour matter but do not change the architecture, and choosing the largest model is a configuration decision that should follow evaluation, not precede it.

why_incorrect.B: Tone is a prompt-level requirement; it is handled in the system prompt and does not change components, data flows or controls.
why_incorrect.D: Model choice is a tunable configuration that should be justified by evaluation results; it is not a structural requirement.
why_incorrect.E: A UI styling preference does not affect the Claude processing architecture.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail's CFO asks whether Claude can 'replace the demand-forecasting system'. The current system is a statistical time-series model that produces SKU-level forecasts nightly with measured error bounds.
questions.question: What is the most appropriate architectural recommendation?

options.A: Replace the forecaster with Claude, prompting it with three years of sales history each night
options.B: Keep the statistical forecaster as the source of numbers and use Claude to explain forecast movements, summarise qualitative signals and answer planner questions against the forecast data
options.C: Replace the forecaster with Claude but ask it to output confidence intervals in a structured schema
options.D: Decline the use case because LLMs cannot work with numeric data

questions.explanation: Part of translating a business problem is recognising where an LLM adds value and where a deterministic or statistical component is the better tool. Numeric time-series forecasting with calibrated error bounds is a strength of the existing statistical system. Claude adds value around it: explaining forecast changes to planners, summarising promotions and supplier notes that affect demand, and turning analyst questions into queries. Replacing a well-performing quantitative model with free-text generation would lose calibration and auditability.

why_incorrect.A: LLMs are not a substitute for calibrated numeric forecasting; this also loses the measured error bounds the business relies on.
why_incorrect.C: A structured schema guarantees the output format, not that the numbers are statistically calibrated.
why_incorrect.D: Claude can reason about and explain numeric data well; the issue is which component should own the forecast, not whether Claude can participate.

questions.scenario: Civic Benefits Agency (a fictional state agency) wants Claude to 'decide' benefit eligibility from uploaded documents to clear a 40,000-application backlog. Eligibility rules are codified in statute and the agency must be able to explain every denial.
questions.question: Which framing should the architect propose?

options.A: Claude reads the statute and the documents and returns an approve/deny decision with a confidence score
options.B: Claude approves clear-cut applications automatically and denies the rest pending appeal
options.C: Claude extracts applicant facts into a validated schema and flags gaps, a rules engine applies the codified eligibility logic, and caseworkers review every proposed denial with Claude-drafted rationale
options.D: Run the backlog through the Batch API with the most capable model to maximise decision accuracy

questions.explanation: When decisions have legal effect and must be explainable, the deterministic rule logic should stay in code where it can be tested and cited, and the model should do what it is good at: extracting facts from messy documents into a validated schema, flagging missing evidence and drafting explanations that cite the rule applied. Denials go to a caseworker. This both clears the backlog (extraction is the slow part) and preserves accountability. Letting the model apply statute directly makes each decision hard to explain and reproduce.

why_incorrect.A: Model confidence scores are not a legal explanation, and letting the model apply statute directly makes decisions hard to reproduce and audit.
why_incorrect.B: Automatic denial with appeal as the only safeguard shifts the burden onto applicants and fails the explainability requirement.
why_incorrect.D: Batch processing addresses cost and throughput, not where decision authority and explainability should sit.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments is designing a merchant-onboarding assistant. Merchants upload business documents; Claude extracts fields; a risk analyst approves; the result is written to the onboarding system. Analysts frequently correct extracted fields.
questions.question: Which design element best closes the feedback loop in this end-to-end architecture?

options.A: Log only whether the analyst clicked approve, to keep storage costs low
options.B: Ask Claude to output a self-assessed confidence per field and skip review above 0.9
options.C: Retrain a custom model weekly on approved records
options.D: Store each analyst correction alongside the original extraction and source reference, and feed these pairs into a regression evaluation set used before every prompt or model change

questions.explanation: An end-to-end design includes a feedback path, not just input, processing and output. Analyst corrections are labelled data: capturing the original extraction, the correction and the document reference lets the team grow a regression eval set, measure field-level accuracy over time and test prompt or model changes before release. Simply logging approvals, or asking the model to self-rate, does not tell you where it was wrong.

why_incorrect.A: A binary approval signal loses which fields were wrong and why, so it cannot drive targeted improvement.
why_incorrect.B: Self-reported confidence is not a calibrated accuracy measure and removing review on that basis weakens a control without evidence.
why_incorrect.C: Claude models are not retrained by customers in this workflow; improvement comes from prompts, context, tooling and evaluation.

questions.scenario: Meridian Clinics is building an intake pipeline: patients submit free-text symptoms through a portal, Claude produces a structured triage record, and the record is inserted into the scheduling database and shown to staff in a web dashboard.
questions.question: Which THREE controls belong in the end-to-end design? (Choose 3.)

options.A: Wrap the patient's text in clearly delimited tags in the prompt and instruct Claude to treat it as data, not instructions
options.B: Use structured outputs for the triage record, then insert it with parameterised queries and HTML-encode fields before rendering in the dashboard
options.C: Accept free-form JSON without a schema so the model can add fields it thinks are useful
options.D: Route any record with red-flag symptom categories to an on-call clinician queue regardless of the model's suggested priority
options.E: Skip output encoding because the content was generated by Claude rather than typed by a user

questions.explanation: Each boundary in an end-to-end pipeline needs its own control. On input, patient text is untrusted and may contain instructions, so it should be delimited as data. On output, a structured-output schema guarantees the record's shape, but downstream systems must still treat it as untrusted: insert with parameterised queries and encode before rendering in HTML. Clinically, urgent cases need a deterministic escalation path rather than relying on the model alone. Removing schema validation 'for flexibility' or trusting model output because it came from Claude both create injection and data-quality risk.

why_incorrect.C: Unconstrained output breaks downstream parsing and lets unexpected fields reach the database and UI.
why_incorrect.E: Model output can carry attacker-controlled text from the input; OWASP treats it as untrusted (improper output handling).

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's statement-analysis service sends long PDFs to Claude and parses the reply. In production, roughly 2% of responses fail to parse and the service writes partial data to the ledger reconciliation table.
questions.question: What is the most robust fix to the processing stage?

options.A: Check `stop_reason` before parsing, handle `max_tokens` and `refusal` explicitly, use structured outputs for the schema, and write nothing to the ledger unless validation passes
options.B: Raise `max_tokens` to the model maximum so responses are never truncated
options.C: Add a regex step that repairs malformed JSON before insertion
options.D: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace to force JSON

questions.explanation: Robust pipelines check why a response ended before using it. A response that stopped with `max_tokens` is truncated; one that stopped with `refusal` has no usable content. The service should branch on `stop_reason`, use structured outputs so successful responses always match the schema, and never write partial results. Larger `max_tokens` alone reduces truncation but does not handle refusals or validation, and regex repair hides real failures.

why_incorrect.B: This reduces one cause but ignores refusals and still writes unvalidated data; it also raises worst-case cost.
why_incorrect.C: Silently repairing output masks truncation and can insert fabricated or partial values into financial records.
why_incorrect.D: Assistant prefill is rejected by current models; structured outputs are the supported way to constrain format.

questions.scenario: Bluefin Grocers wants Claude to generate product descriptions for 250,000 catalogue items overnight, and also to power a live shopper Q&A widget with a sub-two-second first-token target.
questions.question: Which TWO architectural choices best fit these two workloads? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Use the Batch API for the shopper widget too, to halve its cost
options.B: Submit the catalogue generation through the Message Batches API and key results by custom ID
options.C: Run the catalogue job synchronously with fast mode so it finishes sooner
options.D: Serve the shopper widget with streaming from a fast model at low effort, keeping the system prompt stable so it caches
options.E: Use the same synchronous model configuration for both so prompts can be shared

questions.explanation: Different workloads in the same solution deserve different processing paths. The catalogue job is latency-insensitive and high volume, which is exactly what the Message Batches API is for: asynchronous processing at a discount. The live widget needs low time-to-first-token, so streaming responses from a fast, cheaper model at low effort is appropriate, with a stable cached prefix where possible. Running everything synchronously on one model, or batching the live path, ignores the different service levels.

why_incorrect.A: Batch results are asynchronous and cannot meet an interactive latency target.
why_incorrect.C: Fast mode trades a price premium for speed; an overnight job has no latency need and should optimise for cost instead.
why_incorrect.E: Shared prompts do not require identical serving paths, and one configuration cannot satisfy both cost and latency goals well.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing translates manuscripts into four languages. Each translation must then pass a house style checklist, and failed sections are revised until they pass or three attempts are used.
questions.question: Which pattern best describes the appropriate design?

options.A: A single prompt that asks for all four translations and a self-check in one call
options.B: An evaluator-optimizer workflow: generate a translation, evaluate it against the style checklist, feed failures back, and stop after passing or three attempts
options.C: An autonomous agent with a translation tool that decides when the work is finished
options.D: A router that sends each manuscript to the cheapest model that supports the language

questions.explanation: This is the evaluator-optimizer pattern: one step generates, another evaluates against explicit criteria, and the loop repeats with feedback until the criteria pass or a limit is hit. The criteria are clear and the iteration demonstrably improves output. The per-language step can additionally fan out in parallel, but the defining structure is the generate-evaluate loop with a bound. A fully autonomous agent adds unpredictability without benefit when the steps are known.

why_incorrect.A: One call cannot iterate on specific failures, and mixing four languages in one output makes evaluation and retries coarse.
why_incorrect.C: The steps and stopping criteria are known in advance, so ceding control flow to the model adds cost and unpredictability.
why_incorrect.D: Routing addresses model selection, not the requirement to check and revise against a checklist.

questions.scenario: Trey Research's security team wants help investigating alerts. Some alerts need two lookups; others need open-ended exploration across logs, asset inventory and threat intelligence, with an unknown number of steps.
questions.question: Which TWO statements reflect sound pattern selection? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Use a deterministic workflow for alert types with a known, fixed lookup sequence
options.B: Use an agent for every alert because agents are more accurate than workflows
options.C: Start with a multi-agent system so each data source has a dedicated agent
options.D: Use an agent loop with scoped, read-only investigation tools for open-ended alerts where the next step depends on what is found
options.E: Avoid tools and paste all logs into the prompt so the model sees everything

questions.explanation: Agentic patterns earn their cost when the path cannot be specified in advance and the model must decide which tool to call next based on what it finds, which is true for open-ended investigations. Simple, enumerable alert types are better served by a fixed workflow that is cheaper, faster and easier to test. Routing between the two keeps each path appropriate. Agents are not inherently more accurate, and multi-agent designs add coordination cost that needs a reason.

why_incorrect.B: Agents are not inherently more accurate; they trade predictability and cost for flexibility, which simple alerts do not need.
why_incorrect.C: Multi-agent coordination adds tokens and failure modes; it should follow evidence that a single agent is insufficient.
why_incorrect.E: Dumping all logs wastes context and cost and does not scale; scoped retrieval tools are the better pattern.

questions.scenario: Alpine Ski House wants a booking assistant that answers questions about lift passes using the current price list, checks availability via an internal API, and drafts a confirmation email. Each conversation is short.
questions.question: Which description best fits the 'augmented LLM' building block the team should start from?

options.A: A model fine-tuned on historic booking conversations so it no longer needs tools
options.B: A three-agent hierarchy with a planner, a pricing agent and an email agent
options.C: A single Claude call loop given retrieval over the price list and a well-documented availability tool, adding orchestration only if evaluation shows it is needed
options.D: A prompt containing the full price history for every season so no retrieval is needed

questions.explanation: The augmented LLM is the basic building block for both workflows and agents: a model enhanced with retrieval, tools and (where needed) memory, with well-designed interfaces to each. Starting there, with a clear tool contract for availability and retrieval for prices, often covers short conversational tasks without additional orchestration. Fine-tuning, very large static prompts or multi-agent hierarchies are not what the term refers to.

why_incorrect.A: Fine-tuning does not give access to live availability or current prices, which change.
why_incorrect.B: This adds coordination overhead for a short, simple conversation; start with the simplest building block.
why_incorrect.D: Large static context raises cost, risks stale data and does not solve the live availability check.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending runs a document-intake workflow: classify the document type, then apply one of six type-specific extraction prompts. Today every document goes through a single long prompt that covers all six types and accuracy on rare types is poor.
questions.question: Which change best applies an appropriate workflow pattern?

options.A: Parallelise: send every document to all six extraction prompts and keep the most confident result
options.B: An orchestrator-workers agent that decides dynamically how many extraction subtasks to spawn
options.C: Keep the single prompt and add three examples for every document type
options.D: A routing workflow: a lightweight classification step chooses one of six focused extraction prompts, each with its own schema and tests

questions.explanation: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialised follow-up, which lets each prompt stay focused and lets you choose a cheaper or faster model for the classification step. It typically improves accuracy on rare categories that get crowded out in a catch-all prompt. Parallelisation and orchestrator-workers solve different problems, and simply adding examples to the monolith makes it longer without separating concerns.

why_incorrect.A: Running six extractions per document multiplies cost, and model confidence is a weak selector.
why_incorrect.B: The subtasks are known and fixed; dynamic orchestration adds cost without benefit.
why_incorrect.C: Eighteen examples make the catch-all prompt longer and slower without isolating the type-specific logic.

questions.scenario: Adatum Pharma wants a research assistant that answers broad questions such as 'summarise all published evidence on compound class X across five literature databases'. A single agent run fills its context with search results and misses sources.
questions.question: Which orchestration strategy is the most appropriate?

options.A: An orchestrator that plans the search, delegates each database or sub-question to a worker subagent with its own context, and synthesises their condensed findings
options.B: A single agent with a larger context window and instructions to be more thorough
options.C: A sequential chain of five agents, each passing its full transcript to the next
options.D: Five independent agents with no coordinator, whose outputs are concatenated

questions.explanation: Broad, parallelisable research is the case where an orchestrator-worker multi-agent design pays off: a lead agent plans and delegates scoped searches to subagents, each of which explores in its own context window and returns a condensed finding. This keeps the lead's context clean and increases coverage. The cost is higher token usage, which is justified for high-value breadth-first questions. Making one context bigger or chaining sequential agents does not address the context-isolation problem.

why_incorrect.B: A bigger window delays the problem; the agent still accumulates raw results and loses focus.
why_incorrect.C: Passing full transcripts forward recreates the context-bloat problem and removes parallelism.
why_incorrect.D: Without a coordinator there is no plan, deduplication or synthesis, so overlap and gaps go unmanaged.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance runs a lead agent that delegates claim sub-investigations to subagents. Reviews show subagents duplicate each other's work and sometimes investigate the wrong policy period.
questions.question: Which TWO changes most directly address these failures? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Increase effort to max on every subagent
options.B: Make the lead agent's delegation messages explicit about objective, scope boundaries such as policy period, tools to use and output format
options.C: Have the lead partition the investigation into non-overlapping tasks and record which subagent owns each
options.D: Spawn twice as many subagents so coverage improves
options.E: Give every subagent the full transcripts of all other subagents

questions.explanation: Most multi-agent failures trace back to the delegation contract. Each subagent needs a precise task description: objective, scope boundaries (for example the policy period), which tools to use and the expected output format. The lead should also partition work explicitly so tasks do not overlap. Raising effort on subagents or adding more of them does not fix ambiguous instructions, and sharing every transcript defeats context isolation.

why_incorrect.A: Deeper reasoning on an ambiguous task still answers the wrong question and raises cost.
why_incorrect.D: More agents with the same vague instructions increase duplication and cost.
why_incorrect.E: Sharing every transcript floods each context and removes the isolation that makes subagents useful.

questions.scenario: Relecloud's product team proposes splitting a customer-support assistant into seven specialised agents (billing, shipping, returns, and so on) coordinated by a router agent. Each conversation is typically three turns and touches one topic.
questions.question: What is the strongest architectural objection?

options.A: Claude models cannot pass messages between agents
options.B: Short, single-topic conversations do not benefit from parallel exploration, so the extra coordination tokens and failure modes are not justified; a single agent or simple routing to focused prompts is likely sufficient
options.C: Seven agents would exceed the API rate limit
options.D: Specialised agents always produce lower quality than a generalist

questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems multiply token usage and add coordination failure modes; they are justified when tasks are parallelisable, exceed one context, or need many tools that confuse a single agent. Short, single-topic conversations rarely meet that bar. A single agent with topic-specific instructions loaded on demand (for example through Skills or routing to a focused prompt) is cheaper and easier to evaluate. The objection is about fit, not about Claude's inability to coordinate.

why_incorrect.A: Multi-agent orchestration is a supported pattern; the issue is cost and complexity for this workload.
why_incorrect.C: Rate limits are a capacity-planning concern, not the core architectural objection.
why_incorrect.D: Specialisation can help; the objection is that its overhead is not warranted here.

questions.scenario: Proseware is designing a multi-agent system in which a web-research subagent reads arbitrary public pages and a finance subagent can initiate vendor payments. Both report to an orchestrator.
questions.question: Which TWO design decisions best contain the risk of indirect prompt injection spreading across agents? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Add a sentence to every agent's system prompt telling it to ignore instructions found in web pages
options.B: Give all agents a shared scratchpad so the orchestrator can see everything
options.C: Restrict the research subagent to read-only tools and have it return structured findings rather than raw page content
options.D: Gate payment initiation behind a deterministic policy check and human approval, regardless of what upstream agents request
options.E: Use the most capable model for the finance agent so it can recognise malicious instructions

questions.explanation: Content fetched from the web is untrusted and can carry instructions. In a multi-agent system the danger is that such content flows to an agent with consequential tools. Two controls address this: keep the research subagent's tools read-only and have it return structured, summarised findings rather than raw page text, and require that payment actions pass through a deterministic policy check plus human approval that cannot be triggered by text from another agent. Telling agents to 'ignore instructions' helps but is not a boundary, and a shared memory store increases the spread.

why_incorrect.A: Prompt-level instructions reduce but do not reliably prevent injection; they are not an enforcement boundary.
why_incorrect.B: A shared store lets injected text reach the agent holding payment tools more easily.
why_incorrect.E: Model capability is not a security control; consequential actions still need enforced gates.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery's compliance team asks Claude to review distributor contracts: extract key clauses, compare them against a policy playbook, and write a risk memo. A single prompt doing all three produces memos that miss clauses on long contracts.
questions.question: Which decomposition is most effective?

options.A: Keep one call but add 'be thorough and do not miss any clauses' in capitals
options.B: Split the contract into pages and ask for a separate memo per page
options.C: Chain three calls: extract clauses into a structured list, compare the list against the playbook, then draft the memo from the comparison results
options.D: Raise effort on the single call and hope the extra reasoning covers long contracts

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining splits a complex task into sequential subtasks so each call has one clear job and its output can be inspected. Extracting clauses into a structured list first, then comparing that list to the playbook, then drafting the memo from the comparison makes each stage testable and keeps the memo grounded in what was actually extracted. Adding urgency language or asking for more thinking in the same monolithic call does not create checkpoints.

why_incorrect.A: Emphatic wording does not change the task structure and can cause over-triggering on modern models.
why_incorrect.B: Per-page memos lose cross-clause context and still need a merge step that the design does not provide.
why_incorrect.D: More reasoning helps somewhat, but a single call still provides no inspectable intermediate output to verify coverage.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Toys wants Claude to migrate 900 legacy report definitions to a new BI format. Each definition is independent, but the target format has subtle rules learned during the first few conversions.
questions.question: Which THREE decomposition decisions are sound? (Choose 3.)

options.A: Load all 900 definitions into a single request so the model sees the full picture
options.B: Convert a small pilot set first and capture the rules discovered into a shared conversion guide used by every later unit
options.C: Treat each report definition as an independent unit of work that can be processed in parallel or via batch
options.D: Validate each converted definition with a deterministic schema or parser check before accepting it
options.E: Let each conversion infer the target-format rules independently to avoid bias from earlier examples

questions.explanation: Large, homogeneous work decomposes well into independent units that can run in parallel or in batches. Before scaling out, a small pilot surfaces the tricky rules; capturing them in a shared conversion guide (or Skill) gives every unit the same learned context. A deterministic validator per unit makes success objective. Converting everything in one giant context or letting each unit invent its own rules undoes those benefits.

why_incorrect.A: This risks exceeding useful context, makes failures all-or-nothing and gives no per-unit validation.
why_incorrect.E: Rediscovering rules per unit produces inconsistent output; shared, validated guidance is the point of the pilot.

questions.scenario: Margie's Travel built a three-step chain (extract itinerary, check visa rules, draft advice). Customers report wrong visa advice. Logs show the extraction step sometimes outputs the departure country in the 'destination' field.
questions.question: What is the best next step?

options.A: Rewrite the advice-drafting prompt to double-check destinations
options.B: Merge the three steps into one prompt so errors cannot propagate
options.C: Switch the entire chain to a larger model
options.D: Constrain the extraction output with a schema, add a validation check between steps, and add regression cases for the field mix-up

questions.explanation: One advantage of decomposition is that intermediate outputs can be inspected and validated. Here the fault originates in step one and propagates. Adding schema constraints and a validation check (for example, destination must differ from origin and match a country list) at the step boundary, plus targeted test cases, fixes the root cause. Changing the final step or the model treats the symptom.

why_incorrect.A: The final step receives the wrong field; it has no reliable way to detect the upstream error.
why_incorrect.B: Merging removes the inspection point that revealed the bug and makes the failure harder to locate.
why_incorrect.C: The defect is a field-mapping error with a clear root cause; a model change is unjustified without evaluation evidence.

questions.scenario: An architect at Fourth Coffee is deciding whether to decompose a quarterly market-analysis report into subtasks handled by separate calls or to give one agent the whole job.
questions.question: Which TWO factors argue most strongly for decomposition? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Each section requires large, distinct source material that would crowd a single context
options.B: Intermediate results, such as market-size estimates, must be checked or reused by other teams
options.C: The team wants to demonstrate that several different models can be used
options.D: The entire task fits easily in one prompt and the output is short

questions.explanation: Decomposition is worth its overhead when subtasks benefit from separate context (for example, each needs large source material that would crowd others out) and when intermediate results need independent verification or reuse. If the task is small enough to fit comfortably with clear instructions, decomposition adds latency and integration work. Wanting to use more models or to reduce prompt length per se are weak reasons.

why_incorrect.C: Using more models is not a business or quality reason to decompose.
why_incorrect.D: This argues against decomposition, which would add latency and integration overhead for no gain.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's contact centre wants Claude to draft after-call summaries. Agents currently spend six minutes per call on notes. The sponsor wants a business case.
questions.question: Which metric set best demonstrates business value for this efficiency use case?

options.A: Minutes of after-call work saved per call against the current baseline, the share of drafts accepted with minor edits, and fully loaded cost per summary
options.B: Total tokens processed per month and average response latency
options.C: Public benchmark scores of the model chosen
options.D: A survey asking agents whether they like the tool

questions.explanation: Value for an efficiency use case should be measured as outcome per unit of cost, against a baseline: handling time saved, the proportion of drafts accepted with light edits (a quality proxy), and the fully loaded cost per summary including model tokens. Token counts or model benchmark scores alone do not connect to the business outcome, and user enthusiasm is useful but not sufficient.

why_incorrect.B: These are operational metrics; they do not show whether agents save time or whether summaries are usable.
why_incorrect.C: Benchmarks describe general capability, not value in this workflow.
why_incorrect.D: Satisfaction is a useful signal but does not quantify the efficiency gain or quality.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments' fraud-operations VP asks for an availability SLA of 99.99% and a 1-second p95 latency for a Claude-assisted case summariser that analysts open several times an hour.
questions.question: Which TWO responses reflect sound alignment of the solution to its SLA? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Propose graceful degradation so analysts still see raw case data when the model is unavailable, and set the AI component's availability target based on business impact
options.B: Agree to 99.99% because the vendor's API is highly available
options.C: Pre-compute summaries when cases are created and stream on-demand ones, then measure latency per stage against the target
options.D: Meet latency by always using the largest model at max effort and adding retries
options.E: Reject any SLA for AI features because LLM output is non-deterministic

questions.explanation: SLAs should reflect business impact and be engineered across the whole system, not promised for a single dependency. A summariser that supports analysts can degrade gracefully (show raw case data if the model is unavailable), which makes a very high availability target for the AI component unnecessary. Latency targets should be measured per stage, with streaming and pre-computation (generating summaries when cases are created) used to meet perceived latency. Committing to a figure without design, or relying on retries alone, is unsound.

why_incorrect.B: System availability depends on every component and on rate limits; promising a single-dependency figure is not an engineered SLA.
why_incorrect.D: Higher effort and retries usually increase latency rather than reduce it.
why_incorrect.E: Non-determinism affects output content, not whether availability and latency can be targeted and measured.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing's executive team asks whether a proposed Claude rollout is an 'efficiency' or a 'transformation' initiative. The proposal lets editors commission first-draft translations into twelve new languages, opening markets the company never served.
questions.question: How should the architect characterise the value, and why does it matter?

options.A: Primarily efficiency, because translation is faster with AI; success is cost per translated word
options.B: Primarily transformation, because it enables a capability the business did not have; success should be measured by new-market outcomes alongside quality gates, not only cost savings
options.C: Neither; translation is a commodity task with no strategic value
options.D: The distinction does not matter as long as the model is accurate

questions.explanation: Efficiency initiatives do existing work faster or cheaper and are measured against a baseline cost. Transformation initiatives enable work or business models that were not previously viable and are measured by new outcomes such as revenue or market reach. This proposal opens new markets, so the business case, success metrics and risk appetite should reflect transformation: pilot revenue, time-to-market and quality gates per language, not only cost per word.

why_incorrect.A: Cost per word matters, but there is no existing baseline for these twelve languages, so pure efficiency framing misses the value.
why_incorrect.C: Opening new markets is a strategic outcome, so this dismisses the core of the proposal.
why_incorrect.D: The framing determines metrics, investment horizon and risk appetite, so it does matter.
